claim: Eukaryotic ribosomes contain 13 domain-specific proteins.
source: Eukaryotic ribosomes contain 13 domain-specific proteins that may play roles in translation initiation, which is both more complicated and more highly regulated in eukaryotes than in prokaryotes (Ban et al., 2014; Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ban et al., 2014 and Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009.

claim: Translation initiation in eukaryotes is more complicated and more highly regulated than in prokaryotes.
source: Eukaryotic ribosomes contain 13 domain-specific proteins that may play roles in translation initiation, which is both more complicated and more highly regulated in eukaryotes than in prokaryotes (Ban et al., 2014; Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ban et al., 2014 and Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009.

claim: Recruitment of prokaryotic ribosomes to mRNAs requires only three initiation factors, IF1, 2, and 3.
source: Recruitment of prokaryotic ribosomes to mRNAs requires only three initiation factors, IF1, 2, and 3, and relies on base-pairing between the RNA of the small ribosomal subunit and the anti-Shine-Delgarno sequence of the mRNA (Boelens and Gualerzi, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boelens and Gualerzi, 2002.

claim: Prokaryotic ribosome recruitment relies on base-pairing between the RNA of the small ribosomal subunit and the anti-Shine-Delgarno sequence of the mRNA.
source: Recruitment of prokaryotic ribosomes to mRNAs requires only three initiation factors, IF1, 2, and 3, and relies on base-pairing between the RNA of the small ribosomal subunit and the anti-Shine-Delgarno sequence of the mRNA (Boelens and Gualerzi, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boelens and Gualerzi, 2002.

claim: Translation initiation in eukaryotes requires at least 12 initiation factors.
source: In contrast, translation initiation in eukaryotes requires at least 12 initiation factors and proceeds by a complex series of steps beginning with recognition of the mRNA 5′ cap structure, followed by unwinding of mRNA secondary structure, recruitment of the small (40S) ribosomal subunit, scanning, recognition of the initiation codon, and finally, joining of the large (60S) ribosomal subunit to form a functional ribosome (Aitken and Lorsch, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aitken and Lorsch, 2012.

claim: RPL38 is required for the translation of the Hox body-patterning genes during embryonic development.
source: For example, RPL38 is required for the translation of the Hox body-patterning genes during embryonic development, allowing spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression through translational control (Kondrashov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kondrashov et al., 2011.

claim: RPS25, RPL40, and RACK1 are essential for the translation of viral mRNAs that are recruited to the ribosome via alternative initiation pathways.
source: Other proteins including RPS25, RPL40, and RACK1 are essential for the translation of viral mRNAs that are recruited to the ribosome via alternative initiation pathways (Cherry et al., 2005; Landry et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013; Majzoub et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cherry et al., 2005; Landry et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013; Majzoub et al., 2014.

claim: RACK1 is a WD40-repeat β-propeller protein.
source: The eukaryote-specific ribosomal protein RACK1 is a WD40-repeat β-propeller protein that binds the solvent-exposed face of the 40S subunit near the mRNA exit channel, in close proximity to proteins that contact the mRNA during translation initiation (Pisarev et al., 2008; Sengupta et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pisarev et al., 2008 and Sengupta et al., 2004.

claim: RACK1 binds the solvent-exposed face of the 40S subunit near the mRNA exit channel.
source: The eukaryote-specific ribosomal protein RACK1 is a WD40-repeat β-propeller protein that binds the solvent-exposed face of the 40S subunit near the mRNA exit channel, in close proximity to proteins that contact the mRNA during translation initiation (Pisarev et al., 2008; Sengupta et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pisarev et al., 2008 and Sengupta et al., 2004.

claim: In mammalian cells, RACK1 has been found in complex with several proteins involved in signal transduction including protein kinase C, Src kinase, and cAMP phosphodiesterase.
source: In addition to its function as a core ribosomal protein, in mammalian cells, RACK1 has been found in complex with several proteins involved in signal transduction including protein kinase C, Src kinase, and cAMP phosphodiesterase, among many others (Adams et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Adams et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of ASC1 in budding yeast leads to slow growth, loss of invasive growth, loss of cell wall integrity, and decreased 60S subunit levels.
source: Deletion of the RACK1 homolog in budding yeast, ASC1, leads to slow growth, loss of invasive growth, loss of cell wall integrity, and decreased 60S subunit levels, among many described effects (Li et al., 2009; Melamed et al., 2010; Valerius et al., 2007; Yoshikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2009; Melamed et al., 2010; Valerius et al., 2007; Yoshikawa et al., 2011.

claim: In metazoans, RACK1 is required for cell migration, neural tube closure, and control of post-synaptic excitation in the brain.
source: In metazoans, RACK1 is required for cell migration, neural tube closure, and control of post-synaptic excitation in the brain (Kiely et al., 2009; Ron et al., 1999; Wehner et al., 2011; Yaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kiely et al., 2009; Ron et al., 1999; Wehner et al., 2011; Yaka et al., 2002.

claim: Homozygous RACK1 loss-of-function mutations cause early developmental lethality in mouse and flies.
source: These cellular functions may explain why homozygous RACK1 loss-of-function mutations cause early developmental lethality in mouse and flies (Kadrmas et al., 2007; Volta et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kadrmas et al., 2007 and Volta et al., 2013.

claim: Asc1 is required for efficient translation of short mRNAs.
source: Here we have examined the translational functions of Asc1/RACK1 genome-wide by ribosome footprint profiling in yeast ASC1 mutants. We show that Asc1 is required for the efficient translation of short mRNAs, including those encoding cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome footprint profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Asc1 is required for efficient translation of mRNAs encoding cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins.
source: We show that Asc1 is required for the efficient translation of short mRNAs, including those encoding cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome footprint profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ASC1 mutants in S. cerevisiae display compromised translation of specific functional groups, including cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins.
source: ASC1 mutants in S. cerevisiae display compromised translation of specific functional groups, including cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins, and display cellular phenotypes consistent with their gene-specific translation defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome footprint profiling data and GO analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Asc1-sensitive mRNAs are preferentially associated with the translational 'closed loop' complex comprised of eIF4E, eIF4G, and Pab1.
source: Asc1-sensitive mRNAs are preferentially associated with the translational 'closed loop' complex comprised of eIF4E, eIF4G, and Pab1, and depletion of eIF4G mimics the translational defects of ASC1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA immunoprecipitation data from Costello et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of eIF4G mimics the translational defects of ASC1 mutants.
source: Asc1-sensitive mRNAs are preferentially associated with the translational 'closed loop' complex comprised of eIF4E, eIF4G, and Pab1, and depletion of eIF4G mimics the translational defects of ASC1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of data from Park et al., 2011.

claim: The ASC1 locus encodes two distinct gene products — the Asc1 protein and an intronic small nucleolar RNA, snR24.
source: The ASC1 locus encodes two distinct gene products — the Asc1 protein and an intronic small nucleolar RNA, snR24.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ASC1 locus structure.

claim: snR24 directs 2′-O-methylation of 25S rRNA at positions C1437, C1449, and C1450.
source: Because snR24 directs 2′-O-methylation of 25S rRNA at positions C1437, C1449, and C1450, some of the reported phenotypes of ASC1 null mutants (asc1Δ) could be due to effects of deleting SNR24 on ribosome biogenesis or function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about snR24 function.

claim: Both asc1∆ and asc1-M1X showed reduced levels of free 60S subunits.
source: Although bulk polysomes appeared normal in these strains, both asc1∆ and asc1-M1X showed reduced levels of free 60S subunits (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profile data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both asc1-M1X and asc1∆ grow slowly under standard laboratory conditions.
source: Both asc1-M1X and asc1∆ grow slowly under standard laboratory conditions, whereas a mutant lacking only snR24 grows as well as wild type, further demonstrating the importance of the Asc1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A mutant lacking only snR24 grows as well as wild type.
source: Both asc1-M1X and asc1∆ grow slowly under standard laboratory conditions, whereas a mutant lacking only snR24 grows as well as wild type, further demonstrating the importance of the Asc1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Loss of the Asc1 protein caused changes in translation activity for many mRNAs as measured by translational efficiency.
source: Loss of the Asc1 protein caused changes in translation activity for many mRNAs as measured by translational efficiency (TE) — the number of ribosomal footprints normalized by the number of total RNA fragments for each mRNA (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome footprint profiling data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Superficially normal polysomes can conceal significant perturbations of cellular translation.
source: The magnitude and pervasiveness of translation changes in asc1-M1X and asc1Δ are notable given the normal appearance of bulk polysomes in ASC1 mutants (Figure 1D). Thus superficially normal polysomes can conceal significant perturbations of cellular translation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bulk polysomes appear normal while translation efficiency measurements show widespread changes.

claim: Asc1 is a WD-repeat protein that interacts with helices 39 and 40 of the 18S rRNA primarily through its N-terminal blade.
source: Asc1 is a WD-repeat protein that interacts with helices 39 and 40 of the 18S rRNA primarily through its N-terminal blade (Sengupta et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sengupta et al., 2004.

claim: Directed mutation of several basic residues in the N-terminal blade of Asc1 interferes with the ribosome-binding capacity of the protein.
source: Directed mutation of several basic residues in this region interferes with the ribosome-binding capacity of the protein, with the strongest defect observed in the R38D K40E (DE) mutant (Coyle et al., 2009; Sengupta et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coyle et al., 2009 and Sengupta et al., 2004.

claim: The R38D K40E (DE) mutant shows the strongest ribosome-binding defect among Asc1 mutants.
source: Directed mutation of several basic residues in this region interferes with the ribosome-binding capacity of the protein, with the strongest defect observed in the R38D K40E (DE) mutant (Coyle et al., 2009; Sengupta et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coyle et al., 2009 and Sengupta et al., 2004.

claim: The D109Y Asc1 mutant was discovered in a forward genetic screen for mutants with defects in no-go decay.
source: Another Asc1 ribosome-binding mutant, D109Y, was discovered serendipitously in a forward genetic screen for mutants with defects in no-go decay, a ribosome-associated RNA quality control mechanism (Kuroha et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuroha et al., 2010.

claim: Both DE and D109Y mutations substantially decreased co-sedimentation of Asc1 with ribosomes in sucrose gradients, with D109Y having a markedly stronger effect.
source: These mutant proteins were expressed at near wild type levels (Figure 1B), and both mutations substantially decreased co-sedimentation of Asc1 with ribosomes in sucrose gradients, with D109Y having a markedly stronger effect (Figure 2A) that is consistent with previous reports (Kuroha et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Kuroha et al., 2010.

claim: The D109Y strong ribosome-binding mutant showed translational defects that were much smaller in magnitude than those observed in the ASC1 null mutants.
source: The D109Y strong ribosome-binding mutant showed translational defects that, although correlated with those observed in the ASC1 null mutants (r=0.43, p=10–221 for asc1∆; r=0.42, p=10–204 for asc1-M1X), were much smaller in magnitude (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome footprint profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The DE mutant showed almost negligible effects on translation.
source: while the DE mutant showed almost negligible effects on translation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome footprint profiling data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of formaldehyde crosslinking, significant co-sedimentation of the DE and D109Y proteins with polysomes was observed.
source: To test this second possibility, we performed formaldehyde crosslinking before ultracentrifugation. In the presence of crosslinking, we observed significant co-sedimentation of the DE and D109Y proteins with polysomes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ORF length was notably well-correlated with ∆TE in asc1-M1X (r=0.27, p=10–84).
source: Among the tested attributes, ORF length was notably well-correlated with ∆TE in asc1-M1X (r=0.27, p=10–84, Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: ORFs <500 nts were the most strongly affected in asc1-M1X.
source: Among the tested attributes, ORF length was notably well-correlated with ∆TE in asc1-M1X (r=0.27, p=10–84, Table 1) and ORFs <500 nts were the most strongly affected (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Short ORFs are highly translated in wild type cells.
source: Short ORFs are highly translated in wild type cells (Figure 3B and [Arava et al., 2003])
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Arava et al., 2003.

claim: The translational efficiency of the short ORF (~300 nt) was two-fold lower in the asc1-M1X mutant compared to the long ORF (~2400 nt).
source: Remarkably, the translational efficiency of the short ORF (~300 nt) was two-fold lower in the asc1-M1X mutant compared to the long ORF (~2400 nt) (p=0.002, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ORF length reporter experiment data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ORF length is strongly anti-correlated with translational efficiency in diverse eukaryotes.
source: Given that ORF length is strongly anti-correlated with translational efficiency in diverse eukaryotes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D, data from Guo et al., 2010; Stadler and Fire, 2011), this function of Asc1/RACK1 may be conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D and citations to Guo et al., 2010 and Stadler and Fire, 2011.

claim: Asc1's position near the mRNA exit channel places it in close proximity to translation initiation factors that interact with the 5′ end of the mRNA during initiation, including eIF3 and eIF4G.
source: Asc1's position near the mRNA exit channel places it in close proximity to translation initiation factors that interact with the 5′ end of the mRNA during initiation, including eIF3 and eIF4G (Kouba et al., 2012) (Figure 3F
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kouba et al., 2012 and structural information shown in Figure 3F.

claim: eIF4G has a well-characterized role in promoting a circularized form of the mRNA in which the 5′ and 3′ regions of the mRNA are bundled together via the interaction between the eIF4G protein and Pab1.
source: eIF4G has a well-characterized role in promoting a circularized form of the mRNA in which the 5′ and 3′ regions of the mRNA are bundled together via the interaction between the eIF4G protein, associated with the mRNA 5' cap through the eIF4F complex, and Pab1, an RNA-binding protein that binds the poly(A) tail.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eIF4G function.

claim: The mRNA in the circularized conformation is known as the closed loop.
source: The mRNA in this conformation is known as the closed loop, and closed loop formation is thought to enhance translation (Kahvejian et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kahvejian et al., 2001.

claim: Closed loop formation is thought to enhance translation.
source: The mRNA in this conformation is known as the closed loop, and closed loop formation is thought to enhance translation (Kahvejian et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kahvejian et al., 2001.

claim: 'Strong closed loop' and 'closed loop' mRNAs were dramatically shorter than other mRNAs (median ORF lengths= 489, 774, and 1694 nt for 'strong closed loop', 'closed loop', and 'other' mRNAs, respectively).
source: Remarkably, we found that both 'closed loop' and 'strong closed loop' mRNAs were dramatically shorter than other mRNAs (median ORF lengths= 489, 774, and 1694 nt for 'strong closed loop', 'closed loop', and 'other' mRNAs, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA immunoprecipitation data from Costello et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of Asc1 or eIF4G depletion similarly decreased the translation of closed-loop-associated mRNAs.
source: Remarkably, loss of Asc1 or eIF4G depletion (data from Park et al., 2011) similarly decreased the translation of closed-loop-associated mRNAs (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H and I and citation to Park et al., 2011.

claim: Closed loop association has additional explanatory power for translational sensitivity to Asc1 and eIF4G beyond ORF length alone.
source: Accounting for the global relationship between ORF length and ∆TE by linear regression showed that closed loop association has additional explanatory power for translational sensitivity to Asc1 and eIF4G: the observed reductions in translation efficiency for closed-loop-enriched mRNAs were significantly more than would be expected if ORF length alone determined their translation efficiencies (p=10–14 and 10–30 for 'closed loop' and 'strong closed loop' groups, respectively, Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Transcripts annotated to the category 'ribosomal subunit' had significantly decreased TE in the ASC1 null mutants (asc1-M1X, p=10–35).
source: Using gene ontology analysis, we found that transcripts annotated to the category 'ribosomal subunit' had significantly decreased TE in the ASC1 null mutants (asc1-M1X, p=10–35, Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins (RPs, MRPs) both displayed ~20% decreased TE in ASC1 null mutants.
source: This category is composed of short mRNAs encoding both cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins (RPs, MRPs), which both displayed ~20% decreased TE in ASC1 null mutants (asc1-M1X, p=10–37 and p=10–10; asc1∆, p=10–35 and p=10–10, respectively, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The median RP and MRP ORF lengths are 434 and 716 nt, respectively.
source: As the median RP and MRP ORF lengths are 434 and 716 nt, respectively, their translational defects are within the range predicted by their length.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ORF length data.

claim: Removing RP and MRP genes does not significantly alter the global relationship between ∆TE and ORF length in asc1-M1X (r=0.23, p=10–58).
source: Indeed, removing RP and MRP genes does not significantly alter the global relationship between ∆TE and ORF length in asc1-M1X (r=0.23, p=10–58, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RP and MRP mRNAs decreased in both the total RNA pool and the ribosome-protected footprint (FP) pool.
source: We noted that RP and MRP mRNAs decreased in both the total RNA pool and the ribosome-protected footprint (FP) pool (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis of polysome gradient fractions demonstrated that representative MRP mRNAs associated with fewer ribosomes in asc1-M1X.
source: In support of this interpretation, qRT-PCR analysis of polysome gradient fractions demonstrated that representative MRP mRNAs associated with fewer ribosomes in asc1-M1X (Figure 4E,F), which specifically indicates a defect in translation initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Translation efficiency measurements are correlated with steady-state mRNA half-life estimates using non-invasive metabolic labeling approaches.
source: We note that our translation efficiency measurements are correlated with steady-state mRNA half-life estimates using non-invasive metabolic labeling approaches (r=0.43, p=10–194, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, data from Miller et al., 2011 and r=0.39, p=10–168, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, data from Neymotin et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D and citations to Miller et al., 2011 and Neymotin et al., 2014.

claim: None of the tested ribosomal protein mutants (rpl23b∆, rpp1a∆, rps0b∆, rps16b∆) showed notable similarity to asc1-M1X in their translational dysregulation genome-wide.
source: However, none of the tested ribosomal protein mutants showed notable similarity to asc1-M1X in their translational dysregulation genome-wide (r= -0.06 to 0.18, Figure 5A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The tested ribosomal protein mutants (rpl23b∆, rpp1a∆, rps0b∆, rps16b∆) did not display decreased translation efficiency of 'closed loop' mRNAs.
source: and they did not display decreased translation efficieny of 'closed loop' mRNAs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When shifted to glycerol-containing media, wild type yeast resumed rapid growth after an initial adaptation phase, but the asc1-M1X mutant completed only ~3 doublings before ceasing growth.
source: When shifted to glycerol-containing media, wild type yeast resumed rapid growth after an initial adaptation phase, but the asc1-M1X mutant completed only ~3 doublings before ceasing growth (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The rpl23b∆ and rpp1a∆ mutants grew better in glycerol than asc1-M1X.
source: In contrast, the rpl23b∆ and rpp1a∆ mutants grew better in glycerol than asc1-M1X, demonstrating the specificity of this phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A proteomic survey of asc1∆ cells showed a shift away from respiration and towards fermentative metabolism.
source: Consistent with our results, a proteomic survey of asc1∆ cells showed a shift away from respiration and towards fermentative metabolism (Rachfall et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rachfall et al., 2012.

claim: Synthesis of all mitochondrially-translated proteins was reduced >two-fold in asc1-M1X compared to wild type.
source: Synthesis of all mitochondrially-translated proteins was reduced >two-fold in asc1-M1X compared to wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 35S metabolic labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: In the asc1-M1X mutant, polysomes recovered only partially after glucose withdrawal.
source: In the asc1-M1X mutant, polysomes recovered only partially (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profile data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The ribosome-associated pool was strongly depleted of MRP mRNAs in asc1-M1X compared to wild type after shift to glycerol.
source: Moreover, the ribosome-associated pool was strongly depleted of MRP mRNAs compared to wild type (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The magnitude of translational defect (ΔTE) for MRP mRNAs was similar in both glucose and glycerol.
source: However, the magnitude of translational defect (ΔTE) for this class of mRNAs was similar in both glucose and glycerol, supporting a constitutive rather than regulatory role for Asc1 in translation of MRP mRNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Asc1 has a constitutive rather than regulatory role in translation of MRP mRNAs.
source: However, the magnitude of translational defect (ΔTE) for this class of mRNAs was similar in both glucose and glycerol, supporting a constitutive rather than regulatory role for Asc1 in translation of MRP mRNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the magnitude of translational defect is similar in different growth conditions.

claim: A correlation between ORF length and translation efficiency or ribosome density has been observed since the advent of genome-wide translation profiling.
source: A correlation between ORF length and translation efficiency or ribosome density has been observed since the advent of genome-wide translation profiling (Arava et al., 2003; Ingolia et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arava et al., 2003 and Ingolia et al., 2009.

claim: The relationship between ORF length and translation efficiency was observed in data collected from diverse eukaryotes including yeast, nematodes, mice, and humans.
source: and we observed this relationship in data collected from diverse eukaryotes including yeast, nematodes, mice, and humans (Guo et al., 2010; Stadler and Fire, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2010 and Stadler and Fire, 2011.

claim: It was proposed that the rate of translation initiation is higher for short ORFs.
source: To account for this trend, it was proposed that the rate of translation initiation is higher for short ORFs (Arava et al., 2005; Shah et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arava et al., 2005 and Shah et al., 2013.

claim: Short mRNAs preferentially associate with closed loop factors in vivo.
source: Our analyses reveal a clear trend that short mRNAs preferentially associate with closed loop factors in vivo
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA immunoprecipitation data from Costello et al., 2015.

claim: Short mRNAs form more stable closed loop complexes than longer mRNAs in vitro.
source: and consistent with these observations, short mRNAs form more stable closed loop complexes than longer mRNAs in vitro (Amrani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amrani et al., 2008.

claim: eIF4G co-purifies with Asc1 from yeast lysates under stringent conditions in which most other initiation factors do not.
source: Intriguingly, eIF4G co-purifies with Asc1 from yeast lysates under stringent conditions in which most other initiation factors do not (Gavin et al., 2002; 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gavin et al., 2002 and 2006.

claim: Loss of the non-essential ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1 causes a concerted decrease in MRP expression that leads to mitochondrial insufficiency.
source: In particular we show that loss of the non-essential ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1 causes a concerted decrease in MRP expression that leads to mitochondrial insufficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of data including translation efficiency measurements, mitochondrial translation assays, and growth assays on glycerol.

claim: Mitochondrial defects elicit pleiotropic consequences.
source: Given the central role of mitochondria in energy and metabolite production in eukaryotic cells, it is not surprising that mitochondrial defects elicit pleiotropic consequences (Calvo and Mootha, 2010; Fleming et al., 2001; Kushnir et al., 2001; Shoffner et al., 1990; Vafai and Mootha, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calvo and Mootha, 2010; Fleming et al., 2001; Kushnir et al., 2001; Shoffner et al., 1990; Vafai and Mootha, 2012.

claim: Several distinct mutations in human ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis factors result in anemia.
source: Finally, it is intriguing that several distinct mutations in human ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis factors result in anemia, the cause of which is currently the source of much debate (Freed et al., 2010; Narla et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Freed et al., 2010 and Narla et al., 2011.

claim: Many forms of heritable anemia have been traced to defects in mitochondrial iron metabolism.
source: Given that many forms of heritable anemia have been traced to defects in mitochondrial iron metabolism (Dailey and Meissner, 2013; Huang et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dailey and Meissner, 2013 and Huang et al., 2011.

claim: Restoring SNR24 expression rescued the temperature-sensitive polysome defect of the asc1∆ mutant.
source: Restoring SNR24 expression rescued the temperature-sensitive polysome defect of the asc1∆ mutant in agreement with previous observations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D) (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profile data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and citation to Li et al., 2009.

claim: Protein null alleles (asc1-M1X and asc1-E5X) abolished Asc1 protein expression but maintained wild type levels of SNR24.
source: We created protein null alleles by mutating a codon early in the ASC1 ORF to a stop codon (asc1-M1X and asc1-E5X, where X denotes a stop codon), which abolished Asc1 protein expression but maintained wild type levels of SNR24 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: ORF length is slightly more predictive of wild type translation efficiency than transcript length.
source: We then sought to determine whether ORF length or transcript length is more predictive of translational efficiency. ORF length was slightly more predictive of wild type translation efficiency than transcript length, (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E, partial correlation r=-0.09 (p=10–8) vs. r=0.03 (p=10–1)).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E.

claim: The I27 domain from human cardiac protein titin has been used extensively in studies of protein folding because the small globular domains fold and unfold independently of each other.
source: These ORF length reporters contain either one or eight repeats of the I27 domain from the human cardiac protein titin, which has been used extensively in studies of protein folding because the small globular domains fold and unfold independently of each other (Hoffmann and Dougan, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hoffmann and Dougan, 2012.

claim: Most GO categories with short median ORF lengths displayed decreased TE in the ASC1 null mutants, including several additional groups of genes whose protein products function in mitochondria.
source: Although these GO categories were the clear outliers, most GO categories with short median ORF lengths also displayed decreased TE in the ASC1 null mutants, including several additional groups of genes whose protein products function in mitochondria (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibiting translation initiation can induce mRNA degradation.
source: Because inhibiting translation initiation can induce mRNA degradation (Coller and Parker, 2005; LaGrandeur and Parker, 1999; Schwartz and Parker, 1999), decreased translation may account for the reduction in total mRNA levels
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coller and Parker, 2005; LaGrandeur and Parker, 1999; Schwartz and Parker, 1999.

claim: The same trends of decreased TE for the RP and MRP genes were observed using an rRNA-depletion strategy instead of poly(A) selection.
source: The same trends of decreased TE for the RP and MRP genes were observed using an rRNA-depletion strategy instead of poly(A) selection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F), ruling out a significant effect of poly(A) tail length on our ∆TE calculations (Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F and citation to Subtelny et al., 2014.

claim: Asc1 has been implicated in the ribosome-dependent no-go decay pathway.
source: Although Asc1 has been implicated in the ribosome-dependent no-go decay pathway (Kuroha et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuroha et al., 2010.

claim: The observed co-directional changes in mRNA abundance and translational efficiency are not consistent with widespread defects in no-go decay as a driver of changes in translation efficiency.
source: the observed co-directional changes in mRNA abundance and translational efficiency are not consistent with widespread defects in no-go decay as a driver of changes in translation efficiency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mRNA levels decrease rather than increase for genes with decreased TE.

claim: rpl23b∆ and rpp1a∆ show reduced growth on glucose and decreased 60S subunit levels.
source: Like asc1-M1X, rpl23b∆ and rpp1a∆ show reduced growth on glucose and decreased 60S subunit levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve and polysome profile data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: RPS0B and RPS16B encode small ribosomal subunit proteins that bind the ribosome near the mRNA exit channel in the vicinity of Asc1/RACK1.
source: RPS0B and RPS16B encode small ribosomal subunit proteins that bind the ribosome near the mRNA exit channel in the vicinity of Asc1/RACK1 and deletion of these loci results in increased 60S subunit levels relative to 40S levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural information shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and polysome profile data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Deletion of RPS0B and RPS16B loci results in increased 60S subunit levels relative to 40S levels.
source: RPS0B and RPS16B encode small ribosomal subunit proteins that bind the ribosome near the mRNA exit channel in the vicinity of Asc1/RACK1 and deletion of these loci results in increased 60S subunit levels relative to 40S levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profile data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Decreased translation of RP genes is not a general feature of slow-growing mutants, ribosomal subunit imbalance, or perturbations in the vicinity of the mRNA exit channel near RACK1.
source: Thus, decreased translation of RP genes is not a general feature of slow-growing mutants, ribosomal subunit imbalance, or perturbations in the vicinity of the mRNA exit channel near RACK1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that other ribosomal protein mutants with similar phenotypes do not show the same translational defects as asc1-M1X.

claim: Mitochondrial ribosomes are required for mitochondrial biogenesis and function.
source: Because mitochondrial ribosomes are required for mitochondrial biogenesis and function, it is plausible that the growth and metabolic defects of ASC1 mutants are consequences of the translation defects observed for MRP genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial ribosome function.

claim: Adaptation to growth in non-fermentable carbon sources or low glucose is accompanied by a rewiring of the transcriptional network in yeast.
source: Adaptation to growth in non-fermentable carbon sources or low glucose is accompanied by a rewiring of the transcriptional network in yeast (Galdieri et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Galdieri et al., 2010.

claim: Adaptation to growth in non-fermentable carbon sources or low glucose is accompanied by widespread reprogramming of translation.
source: and widespread reprogramming of translation (Vaidyanathan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vaidyanathan et al., 2014.

claim: The cellular context is an important factor in determining the phenotypic consequences of translational perturbations in asc1-M1X and likely in other ribosomal protein mutants as well.
source: Thus, the cellular context is an important factor in determining the phenotypic consequences of translational perturbations in asc1-M1X and likely in other ribosomal protein mutants as well.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that asc1-M1X shows different phenotypes in glucose versus glycerol.

claim: Asc1/RACK1 plays a role in a length-dependent initiation mechanism optimized for efficient translation of genes with important housekeeping functions.
source: Together our results reveal a role for Asc1/RACK1 in a length-dependent initiation mechanism optimized for efficient translation of genes with important housekeeping functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of data including ORF length analysis, reporter assays, and functional characterization.

claim: The presence of a ribosome-dependent regulatory mechanism specifically enhances the translation of short mRNAs by promoting the formation and/or function of the closed loop.
source: Our results add an additional nuance to these physical models — the presence of a ribosome-dependent regulatory mechanism that specifically enhances the translation of short mRNAs by promoting the formation and/or function of the closed loop.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that short mRNAs are enriched with closed loop factors and require Asc1 for efficient translation.

claim: Asc1 may interact directly with the closed loop via eIF4G.
source: Intriguingly, eIF4G co-purifies with Asc1 from yeast lysates under stringent conditions in which most other initiation factors do not (Gavin et al., 2002; 2006), suggesting that Asc1 may interact directly with the closed loop via eIF4G.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on co-purification data from Gavin et al., 2002 and 2006.

claim: Translation of many mRNAs could be co-regulated by mechanism(s) that target Asc1/RACK1's function in closed-loop-dependent initiation.
source: Our results also raise the possibility that translation of many mRNAs could be co-regulated by mechanism(s) that target Asc1/RACK1's function in closed-loop-dependent initiation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the findings about Asc1's role in closed-loop-dependent translation.

claim: Many of Asc1/RACK1's ascribed cellular functions should be re-evaluated for potential connections to mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: In light of our findings, many of Asc1/RACK1's ascribed cellular functions should be re-evaluated for potential connections to mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the finding that loss of Asc1 causes mitochondrial insufficiency.

claim: Signaling pathways in yeast and human have diverged significantly compared to genes required for ribosomal function.
source: However, signaling pathways in yeast and human have diverged significantly compared to genes required for ribosomal function (Stuart et al., 2003), suggesting that RACK1 might have another, more conserved function during translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stuart et al., 2003.

claim: ~30% of the 'strong closed loop' mRNAs encode ribosomal proteins.
source: Thus, although ~30% of the 'strong closed loop' mRNAs encode ribosomal proteins, a specialized mechanism for enhancing the translation of ribosomal protein mRNAs cannot explain the ORF length bias of the 'strong closed loop' group.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of closed loop association data from Costello et al., 2015.

claim: A specialized mechanism for enhancing the translation of ribosomal protein mRNAs cannot explain the ORF length bias of the 'strong closed loop' group.
source: Thus, although ~30% of the 'strong closed loop' mRNAs encode ribosomal proteins, a specialized mechanism for enhancing the translation of ribosomal protein mRNAs cannot explain the ORF length bias of the 'strong closed loop' group.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the ORF length bias persists even when ribosomal protein mRNAs are excluded from the analysis.

claim: The association between ORF length and closed loop association was observed regardless of whether mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins were included in the analysis.
source: This association between ORF length and closed loop association was observed regardless of whether mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins were included in the analysis (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The discovery that closed-loop-associated mRNAs are much shorter than other mRNAs provides a plausible biochemical explanation for the preference for higher translation efficiency of mRNAs with short ORFs.
source: This discovery — that closed-loop-associated mRNAs are much shorter than other mRNAs — provides a plausible biochemical explanation for the preference for higher translation efficiency of mRNAs with short ORFs observed here and previously (Arava et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that short mRNAs are enriched with closed loop factors and closed loop formation enhances translation.

claim: All classes of genes with short ORFs have decreased TE in asc1-M1X.
source: Indeed, removing RP and MRP genes does not significantly alter the global relationship between ∆TE and ORF length in asc1-M1X (r=0.23, p=10–58, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) indicating that all classes of genes with short ORFs have decreased TE in asc1-M1X.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the relationship between ∆TE and ORF length persists after removing RP and MRP genes.

claim: Loss of Asc1 leads to coherent changes in gene expression because short ORF length is associated with specific functional categories.
source: Because short ORF length is associated with specific functional categories, loss of Asc1 — and, potentially, modulation of its activity — leads to coherent changes in gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that genes with short ORFs cluster into functional categories and show coordinated changes in translation efficiency.

claim: The fact that asc1-M1X shows a bulk translation defect in glycerol but not in glucose may reflect the fact that MRP mRNAs make up a larger portion of the translatome in glycerol.
source: The fact that asc1-M1X shows a bulk translation defect in glycerol but not in glucose may reflect the fact that MRP mRNAs make up a larger portion of the translatome in glycerol.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of different polysome profiles in glucose versus glycerol.

claim: The pleiotropic phenotypes associated with the Asc1/RACK1 protein should be re-examined in the context of mitochondrial health.
source: Furthermore, because mitochondria are essential for energy generation and regulation of many cellular networks, our results suggest that the pleiotropic phenotypes associated with the Asc1/RACK1 protein should be re-examined in the context of mitochondrial health.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the finding that loss of Asc1 causes mitochondrial insufficiency.
